one_line: Better Stack walkthrough of PG Durable, a Microsoft open-source Postgres extension for crash-proof durable functions, scheduling, retries and human-in-the-loop approval in plain SQL.
summary: The video introduces PG Durable, an open-source Postgres extension from Microsoft that persists workflow steps to disk so long-running jobs survive database restarts. Workflows are written as a graph of steps in a SQL DSL and submitted with df.start, which returns an 8-character id that can be checked with df.status or read with df.results. Built-in operators cover sequencing, parallel execution, racing, looping, conditionals, variable assignment, signal waits and cron-style waits (df.waitForSchedule). The demos show a loop that refreshes a materialized view on a one-minute schedule with no external scheduler, and an order-approval workflow that parks for up to 24 hours until df.signal wakes it. A Docker Compose setup runs the Microsoft image on Postgres 17 with shared_preload_libraries set to pgdurable. The speaker claims a 300-line SQL boilerplate example on the project site shrinks to seven lines, with retries and error handling handled by the extension. The video is a short, demo-led overview; it does not test crash recovery, scale or operational cost.

key_ideas.idea: Durable functions persist every step to disk, which gives crash and restart guarantees a plain BEGIN/COMMIT block or cron job does not.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker contrasts durable steps with a transaction or cron job: database crashes, restarts, long waits and failures are handled inside Postgres, with no external workflow service.

key_ideas.idea: Workflows are submitted from SQL with df.start and tracked by id.
key_ideas.detail: df.start returns an 8-character id. df.status reports operation state and df.results returns the final output once complete. A trivial SELECT wrapped in df.start shows the pattern.

key_ideas.idea: Scheduling without an external service is built from a loop of sequenced steps.
key_ideas.detail: The demo wraps a loop around a sequence: wait one minute, then call a procedure that refreshes materialized views and inserts a row into a log table. The job keeps firing for as long as the database runs it, and the demo shows three log rows after a few minutes.

key_ideas.idea: Human-in-the-loop approval is a parked workflow that a signal wakes.
key_ideas.detail: The order workflow selects the top order into a variable, waits up to 24 hours for a signal stored in a second variable, then uses an if to set the order to approved or rejected. The first process exits once df.signal is called from a separate approval script.

key_ideas.idea: Built-in operators replace hand-written queue, worker and retry code.
key_ideas.detail: Operators cover sequence, parallel (ampersand), race (fastest result wins), loop, if, wait-for-signal and wait-for-schedule. Error handling and retries are described as automatic, not user-coded.

key_ideas.idea: Local setup is a single Postgres 17 container with the extension preloaded.
key_ideas.detail: The compose file uses the Microsoft PG Durable image on Postgres 17 and sets shared_preload_libraries to pgdurable. The rest of the config is standard and can be changed freely.

techniques.name: Run a recurring job inside Postgres
techniques.how: Submit SELECT df.start(...) wrapping a loop operator around a sequence: a one-minute wait, then a procedure call (the demo calls a refresh-materialized-views procedure that inserts into a refresh_log table). Keep the start script running; the workflow persists and fires on the schedule. Check progress with a SELECT on the log table ordered by id. For cron-style timing, the speaker names df.waitForSchedule.
techniques.when: Replacing an external cron, queue or scheduler for in-database maintenance jobs such as refreshes, rollups or cleanup.

techniques.name: Park a workflow until a human approves
techniques.how: Workflow: SELECT the next pending record into a variable; sequence a wait for an approval signal with a 24-hour timeout, stored in a second variable; use an if to set status to approved or rejected based on the signal and timeout. Approval side: call df.signal with the workflow id and the decision payload. The original df.start process exits once the signal arrives.
techniques.when: Approval gates where the process must not hold a connection or worker while waiting, such as order approvals or review steps.

techniques.name: Fan out and fan in
techniques.how: Combine operations with the ampersand operator to run them in parallel, then sequence a final step (the demo refreshes a dashboard after three parallel operations). The exact DSL syntax for each operator is not shown on screen; see the project docs linked in the description.
techniques.when: Several independent refresh or fetch steps followed by one dependent step.

techniques.name: Local dev via Docker Compose
techniques.how: Use the Microsoft PG Durable image (Postgres 17). Add shared_preload_libraries=pgdurable under command, keep other settings default, and start the container. Run the example scripts from npm (the demo uses npm run workflow) against it.
techniques.when: Trying PG Durable locally before deciding whether to adopt it.

tools: PG Durable (pgdurable, Postgres extension, Microsoft, open source)

numbers.claim: Durable function ids are 8 characters, returned by df.start.
Approval wait times out after 24 hours.
Demo schedule fires every minute; three log rows were visible after a few minutes of running.
Site example claims a 300-line SQL boilerplate (queues, workers, polling, retries, state tracking) reduces to seven lines with PG Durable.

hot_takes: The 300-to-7-line reduction is a claim from the project site, shown as a slide, not a measured result in the video.
The video calls the workflows crash-proof and describes retries as automatic, but it does not demonstrate a crash, a retry or a failure.
Running long workflows inside the database may trade app-tier scaling for DB load; the video does not discuss this.
Overview quality is decent for a short demo-led intro, but it is a product walkthrough of a Microsoft project with no sponsor disclosure and no comparison to pgmq, Temporal or similar.

relevance.why: Durable state, signal-based resume and in-DB scheduling overlap with the storage layer (Postgres, Redis) and any long-running agent job handling, but AgentOS does not currently need a database-hosted workflow engine.
relevance.action: Test PG Durable's signal and wait-for-schedule operators against a long-running agent job locally before deciding whether a durable-execution layer belongs in the storage tier.

relevance.why: Checkpoint/resume of long agent runs and phone-driven approvals map directly onto parked workflows woken by a signal, and waitForSchedule maps onto ProsHarness loops and schedules.
relevance.action: Compare PG Durable's park-and-signal approval pattern with ProsHarness's checkpoint/resume and phone approval flow, and note what a Postgres-backed checkpoint store would need (state schema, signal payload, timeout behavior).
